title: The Mill on the Floss: A Literary Discussion

segments.title: Opening: The Mill, the Family, and What They Stand to Lose

utterances.text: Welcome to The Mill on the Floss Unpacked.
I'm your host, and over the course of this series we're going to take George Eliot's great novel apart — passage by passage, argument by argument — and put it back together again.
This is a novel about a family, a river, a mill — and the slow, terrible accumulation of forces that destroy all three.
It's also one of the funniest books in English literature, and one of the most heartbreaking.
Today we begin at the beginning — the world of the Tullivers and their extended family, and what they stand to lose.
Joining me today are three remarkable readers, each bringing a completely different set of tools to the text.

Dr. Daniel Rosen is a cultural historian who reads every novel as an anatomy of class power — who the system protects, who it grinds down, and how literature both reflects and sometimes resists that machinery.
Daniel, welcome.

Professor James Blackstone is a legal and social historian — the person in the room who can tell you exactly what the law meant for ordinary people in Eliot's England, and why that matters enormously for this novel.
James, great to have you.

And Oliver Trevelyan is an actor and writer — the voice behind more classic novel audiobooks than seems humanly possible — who comes to fiction as a performer first, hearing the rhythms and comic timing that live inside the prose.
Oliver, delighted you're here.
Let's begin with the world Eliot constructs around the Tulliver family — the provincial town of St Ogg's, the merchant class, the respectable relations who will prove so consequential.
James, you've been looking closely at Mr Glegg — one of the Dodson uncles — and I think he gives us a wonderfully precise portrait of a whole social type.
He does — and Eliot is extraordinarily exact about him.
Mr Glegg is a retired wool merchant, comfortable but not grand — and that distinction matters enormously in this world.
Eliot places him in the generation of men who made their modest fortunes slowly, by accumulation rather than speculation.
She's precise about the sociology of thrift — and she's precise about its limits.
There's a passage I keep returning to, where she describes Glegg's habits of saving as belonging to
"the industrious men of business of a former generation, who made their fortunes slowly, almost as the tracking of the fox belongs to the harrier."
That simile — the harrier tracking the fox — tells you everything about the tempo of that world.
It's patient, methodical, and it doesn't rush — because it doesn't need to.
And Eliot is already mourning that world, even as she's satirising it.
What I love is that she gives Glegg an entire inner life built around his own bewilderment.
He's retired, he has time to think — and what he thinks about is caterpillars, slugs, and Mrs Glegg.
Those two mysteries occupy him with equal seriousness, and Eliot plays it completely straight.
But the real comic masterpiece is the line about marriage.
She writes — and I could recite this in my sleep —

"That a creature made — in a genealogical sense — out of a man's rib, and in this particular case maintained in the highest respectability without any trouble of her own, should be normally in a state of contradiction to the blandest propositions."
"In a genealogical sense" — that parenthetical is doing the work of an entire essay on Victorian gender ideology, and she buries it in a subordinate clause.
Genius, frankly.
I'd push on that slightly — because what Eliot is doing with Glegg isn't just comic portraiture.
She's anatomising the ideology of the respectable provincial middle class at a precise historical moment.
Notice that Glegg is perfectly capable of feeling something at the sale of a widow's furniture — but he won't pay the five pounds to stop it.
Eliot describes his idea of charity as — and this is verbatim —
"a contribution of small aids, not a neutralizing of misfortune."
That is the operating principle of an entire class — and it will bear directly on what happens to the Tulliver family.
The Gleggs of the world are always willing to feel sympathy — and always unwilling to spend it.
That's precisely right — and there's a legal dimension to it that I think goes unnoticed.
Glegg's thrift isn't merely personal temperament — it's the rational response of a man who knows exactly how the law of debt works and what it can strip away.
In this period, a businessman's entire household could be dismantled by creditors — the furniture, the stock, everything.
Glegg's meanness is a form of armour — and the novel knows it.
Which makes the comedy darker than it first appears, doesn't it.
You're laughing at Glegg and his slugs, and then you realise this is the man who will decide whether the Tullivers keep their home.
That's Eliot's structural genius — the comedy and the tragedy are built from exactly the same materials.
And speaking of the materials — Daniel, you've been looking at a passage that gives us Eliot operating in quite a different register: Tom Tulliver as a young man on the make.
What did you find there?
It's a brief passage, but it's a perfect miniature — Eliot at her most wickedly knowing about class mobility.
Tom is in small lodgings, working his way up — and Maggie laughs at him, retreats, and he flings the bell-rope across the room in frustration.
And the narrator steps in with this extraordinary aside — addressed directly to the reader.
She writes:

"not very far either,— a touch of human experience which I flatter myself will come home to the bosoms of not a few substantial or distinguished men who were once at an early stage of their rise in the world, and were cherishing very large hopes in very small lodgings."
"Very large hopes in very small lodgings" — that's the entire tragicomedy of social aspiration in nine words.
And notice what she's doing: she's implicating her reader — the substantial or distinguished man — in Tom's cramped ambition.
She's saying: you got out. Tom may not.
"I flatter myself" — it's such a teasing phrase from a narrator who is never actually flattering herself.
She knows exactly what she's doing, and the false modesty is part of the wit.
Performing humility is its own kind of power.
There's something historically very pointed about the phrase "rise in the world" too.
In the 1820s and 1830s — the novel's period — that rise was genuinely possible for men of Tom's background, but it required the suppression of almost everything else.
Including, perhaps, one's sister.
Precisely — and that suppression lands with full force later in the novel, when Maggie is paying the price for choices that Tom would never have been required to make.
There's a passage I want to bring in here — from much later, after Maggie's elopement with Stephen Guest.
She wakes in the early hours, and the full weight of what she has done arrives.
Eliot writes:
"she had brought sorrow into the lives of others,— into the lives that were knit up with hers by trust and love."
"Knit up" — it's not a metaphor chosen carelessly.
To be knit to someone is to be structurally entangled — and Maggie is discovering that the entanglements which defined her were not constraints she could simply choose to leave.
The system that confined her also made her who she is.
That dream sequence that precedes it is one of the most extraordinary pieces of writing in the book.
She sees Lucy in the dream as the Virgin in St Ogg's boat — her brother rowing past without looking at her.
And then what Eliot calls "the soothed sense of that false waking" — that moment of relief before the real waking comes — is unbearable.
It's the cruelty of hope — the brief reprieve — before the awful starlit sky.
And that waking — that moment of reckoning — is where we begin to see the full cost of everything the novel has been building.

The comedy of the Gleggs and the tragedy of Maggie Tulliver are woven from the same fabric — a world of provincial respectability that offers almost no room for a woman who thinks and feels as she does.
We'll be exploring that world in much greater depth throughout this series.
After the break, we turn to the Tulliver household itself — and to the fateful decisions that set everything in motion.

segments.title: The Weight of Expectation: Maggie's Intellectual Hunger Against Convention

utterances.text: Welcome to The Mill on the Floss Unpacked.
I'm your host, and today we're diving into one of the great English novels — George Eliot's story of a family, a river, and a young woman who contains more life than her world can hold.
We're exploring the weight of expectation — what Eliot does with characters who are crushed by forces larger than themselves, and what it costs to feel as much as Maggie Tulliver feels.
Joining me today are three people who bring very different and very sharp lenses to this novel.
Dr Daniel Rosen is a cultural historian who reads fiction as an anatomy of class power — he'll show us what the novel's institutions are actually doing to the people caught inside them.
Professor James Blackstone is a legal and social historian — he brings the real-world texture of Victorian life, the law, the money, the machinery of ruin.
And Oliver Trevelyan is an actor and writer who has narrated more classic novels than almost anyone alive — he hears what Eliot wrote for the voice, and he'll read it accordingly.
Let's begin with the fathers — and specifically with the trap Mr Tulliver walks into with his eyes, if not quite open, then at least pointed in entirely the wrong direction.
What Eliot does with Mr Tulliver is almost Sophoclean in its precision.
He is not a weak man — Eliot is absolutely insistent on that point.
His will is not feeble.
And yet the structure of the world he inhabits — the market, the legal system, the narrow pool of available capital — makes his resistance meaningless.
She sets it up like this:
"Mr Tulliver had a destiny as well as Œdipus, and in this case he might plead, like Œdipus, that his deed was inflicted on him rather than committed by him."
That word — inflicted — is doing enormous work.
It relocates the origin of suffering outside the self.
And by reaching for Oedipus, Eliot is saying: the forces that destroy Mr Tulliver are not personal failings — they are systemic, structural, and in a very real sense ancient.
And we should be clear about what that system actually was.
In the early decades of the nineteenth century, the market for private lending was extraordinarily thin in provincial England.
There was no high street bank to walk into.
You needed someone with capital who was willing — and typically that meant someone already embedded in the local legal and commercial network.
Wakem being a lawyer is not incidental — he sits at the centre of exactly that web.
Tulliver's hatred of Wakem is not irrational — it's the hatred of a man who can see the trap closing and cannot find any door that doesn't lead back into it.
What I find devastating — and Eliot is very funny about it before she's devastating — is that Tulliver spends a fortnight convincing himself he has options.
A whole fortnight of magnificent, useless will.
And then: external fact was stronger.
Five words, in the narrator's driest voice, and the whole edifice of his resistance collapses.
Eliot is a comedian of inevitability — she makes you laugh and then makes you feel awful about having laughed.
That comedy of inevitability has a counterpart in tenderness, though — and Eliot holds both at once.
There's a passage about Tom coming home from school — about what home means when it is the place you were formed.

"There is no sense of ease like the ease we felt in those scenes where we were born, where objects became dear to us before we had known the labour of choice, and where the outer world seemed only an extension of our own personality."
The labour of choice — that phrase stops me every time.
What Eliot is identifying is that the home the Tullivers are about to lose is not merely a building.
It is the pre-rational ground of their selves — the thing that existed before they had any consciousness of choosing it.
To strip that away is not just impoverishment — it is a kind of ontological violence.
Ontological violence is precisely the right phrase for what bankruptcy proceedings did to a family in this period.
The contents of the house were inventoried and sold — and Eliot's line about furniture put up to auction is not decorative.
That is exactly what happened.
The rug, the grate, the fire-irons — those objects Eliot lists — would have been assessed and tagged and carried out.
What the law saw as recoverable assets, the family experienced as the dismemberment of identity.
The distance between those two perspectives — the creditor's ledger and the family's grief — is one of the central moral distances of the novel.
And Eliot knows that the grief is particular — rooted in specific, almost laughable objects.
She says that furniture might look very commonplace, even ugly, at auction — and an improved taste in upholstery scorns it.
There's a magnificent little spike of sarcasm in that — a nursery-gardener's contempt for the elderberry bush.
But then she turns it: the elderberry bush is the long companion of my existence, that wove itself into my joys when joys were vivid.
And there it is — one of those sentences where the rhythm itself performs the emotion it describes.
That weight of accumulated attachment — the things that make us who we are before we know it — press hardest on Mr Tulliver himself at the very end of his life.
Daniel, you've been looking at two moments where Tulliver speaks in the full knowledge that he is a broken man.
They are two of the most quietly shattering lines in the novel.
The first is to Maggie — just five words, delivered without melodrama:
"Ay, my little wench, but I shall never live twice o'er."
Eliot doesn't frame it, doesn't comment on it — she just sets it down and moves on.
The plainness of the dialect — ay, my little wench — is doing everything.
It situates the man in his class, his region, his whole formation — and then the sentence beneath it tolls like a bell.
The second is to Bessy and Tom together — and it has the same quality of absolute, undramatised finality:
"We shall never be young again — this world's been too many for me."
This world's been too many for me.
That idiom — being too many — it means overpowered, overwhelmed, outmanoeuvred.
Tulliver is not asking for pity — he is making an accurate statement of the balance of forces.
When you perform that line, you have to resist every temptation to colour it.
Any tremor in the voice, any reaching for pathos, and it collapses into sentimentality.
The power is entirely in the flatness — the way a man states a fact he has known for a long time and is only now saying aloud.
Eliot understood — better than almost any novelist I've read — that the most devastating lines are the ones that don't ask you to weep.
And both lines speak to the particular experience of a man of Tulliver's generation and class.
For men like him, there was no second act.
There was no mechanism for recovery — no bankruptcy protection in any meaningful modern sense, no safety net, no means of starting again with credit intact.
Once the mill was gone and the debts were registered, his social existence — his identity as a man of independent standing — was simply over.
I shall never live twice o'er isn't resignation — it's a precise legal and social fact.
The system that crushes Tulliver also shapes his daughter — and Maggie's struggle is both less visible and, in many ways, more acute.
Daniel, you've been looking at a passage where that interior struggle becomes almost physical.
This is one of the most honest passages about moral struggle in Victorian fiction.
Maggie has retreated to her room after Tom's cruelty to Philip — and she tries to recover the serenity she once felt.
But Eliot refuses to let her — and refuses to let us — settle into comfortable penitence.
Listen to the full weight of this:
"She used to think in that time that she had made great conquests, and won a lasting stand on serene heights above worldly temptations and conflict.
And here she was down again in the thick of a hot strife with her own and others' passions."
Serene heights — that is the language of renunciation literature, of the spiritual manuals Maggie was reading.
Eliot lets Maggie inhabit that language — and then she punctures it utterly.
And then comes the line that has no parallel in Victorian writing for its somatic rawness:

"Her heart bled for Philip; she went on recalling the insults that had been flung at him with so vivid a conception of what he had felt under them, that it was almost like a sharp bodily pain to her, making her beat the floor with her foot and tighten her fingers on her palm."
Beat the floor with her foot.
That is empathy rendered as involuntary physical convulsion — and in 1860, to write that of a woman is a radical act.
That line is almost impossible to read aloud without pausing afterward.
Not for effect — but because the body of the reader responds to it in some way.
There's a rhythm to it — tighten her fingers on her palm — that enacts the very tension it describes.
Eliot wrote for the voice before she wrote for the eye — and this is the proof.
What strikes me in that passage is the word obstructed — her penitence and submission were constantly obstructed by resentment.
Eliot is making a very specific moral distinction: Maggie cannot simply submit because her submission would be false — built on a misattribution of fault.
Tom was not entirely right.
And Eliot will not allow the narrative to pretend otherwise, even for the sake of Maggie's spiritual comfort.
There is more moral realism in that one passage than in any three chapters of most Victorian novels.
And that realism extends to those who try to help Maggie — with equally honest results.
There's a passage about Dr Kenn — after Maggie has left him — that I find almost unbearable in its clarity.
He can see that marriage to Stephen might be the least harmful outcome.
But he also sees something more important than consequences:
"Her conscience must not be tampered with; the principle on which she had acted was a safer guide than any balancing of consequences."
A safer guide than any balancing of consequences.
Eliot is arguing — through Kenn's paralysis — that utilitarian calculation is not a substitute for moral integrity.
The system will always offer a convenient arrangement — and Maggie's greatness is precisely that she refuses it.
Kenn is in an impossible position — and Eliot is completely honest about why.
Every practical path available to Maggie involves a cost to someone else — Lucy, Philip, Stephen, herself.
Eliot uses a remarkable phrase: each immediate step was clogged with evil.
Clogged — it's a mechanical image, almost industrial.
The moral world, like the economic world, is a mechanism that jams — and the people caught in it are not villains, they are simply ground down.
Kenn standing there ruminating with his hands behind him and his eyes fixed on the carpet — it's one of those moments where Eliot's physical detail is devastating.
He's not a weak man, not a bad man — he is a good man in a situation that goodness cannot solve.
And Eliot frames it with that phrase — painful sense of doubt and difficulty.
No resolution, no comfort — just the honest acknowledgement that sometimes the darkness is impenetrable.
This world's been too many for me — and perhaps too many for Kenn, and too many for Maggie herself.
What Eliot refuses — and what makes this novel so unsparing — is any exit from that complexity that doesn't cost something real.
Daniel, James, Oliver — thank you for this.
We'll continue our exploration of The Mill on the Floss in the next segment.

segments.title: A House Divided: Tom and Maggie's Fracturing Loyalty

utterances.text: Welcome back to The Mill on the Floss Unpacked.
We're turning now to one of the novel's deepest wounds — the fracturing bond between Tom and Maggie Tulliver.
Their relationship is, in many ways, the emotional engine of the entire book.
And yet it is also a site of tremendous cruelty — cruelty dressed up as duty, as protection, as love.
To guide us through it, I'm joined by Dr. Daniel Rosen, who reads the novel as an anatomy of the systems that constrain lives like Maggie's.
By Prof. James Blackstone, who brings the legal and social scaffolding of the period into sharp focus.
And by Oliver Trevelyan, who hears this novel as a performer — alive to every rhythm, every pause, every comic and tragic register.
Daniel, I want to start with you — and with Tom.
Because Eliot introduces him with this quietly devastating observation about what ordinary boyish faces conceal.
What does that passage tell us about the architecture of destiny in this novel?
What Eliot is doing there is extraordinarily subversive, and I think readers often sail past it.
She's dismantling the comfortable Victorian assumption that character is legible — that you can read a person's destiny in their face, their manner, their sex.
Maggie is dark, intense, visibly marked by nature — and so the world reads her as the dangerous, unpredictable one.
Tom is pink-and-white, bland, unremarkable — and so the world reads him as safe.
And then Eliot drops this in — almost as an aside.
"Under these average boyish physiognomies that she seems to turn off by the gross, she conceals some of her most rigid, inflexible purposes, some of her most unmodifiable characters."
The word 'unmodifiable' is the one that arrests me every time.
Because Tom's tragedy — and Maggie's — is precisely that he cannot be changed by experience, by love, by suffering.
And Eliot tells you that in the very first chapters — she tucks the whole tragedy into a parenthesis about a boy staring at lambs.
That's the genius of it — the comic surface and the terrible undertow running simultaneously.
I've read this aloud many times, and I always feel the joke of the goslings — a lad who looks like every other lad — and then the ground shifts beneath your feet.
'The dark-eyed, demonstrative, rebellious girl may after all turn out to be a passive being' — Eliot says it straight out.
And of course Maggie is not passive — but what kills her is the passivity that the world demands of her.
That reading holds, but I'd add a legal and institutional dimension.
The 'unmodifiability' Daniel identifies in Tom is not just a character trait — it is the disposition that the period's legal and financial structures actively rewarded.
Consistency, inflexibility, rule-following — these were the virtues of the counting house and the court of equity alike.
Tom is, in a sense, perfectly constituted for the world he will inherit — at Maggie's expense.
James, that's exactly right — and it takes us straight to the confrontation in chapter thirty-seven.
Because there we see Tom's inflexibility deployed as a weapon — not only against Maggie, but against Philip Wakem, using the full arsenal of class, honour, and bodily contempt.
Tom forces Maggie to swear on a Bible — a deeply coercive act dressed as moral rigour.
And the terms he uses to justify it are worth sitting with.

"I can't trust you, Maggie. There is no consistency in you... while I have been contriving and working that my father may have some peace of mind before he dies,—working for the respectability of our family,—you have done all you can to destroy both."
Respectability — that word does the work of ten arguments.
It is the coin of class aspiration — and Tom is paying off the family debt by spending Maggie's freedom.
What I find almost unbearable — in the best theatrical sense — is that Tom believes every word of it.
He is not performing villainy. He is performing righteousness — and he has cast Maggie as the threat to the performance.
And then there's the moment he turns on Philip — and the language changes register completely.
"I'll save her from throwing herself away on you,—from making herself a laughing-stock,—from being flouted by a man like your father, because she's not good enough for his son."
There's something almost medieval about that speech — the honour culture, the family bloodline, the taint of unworthiness.
Eliot writes it with extraordinary economy — you see Tom, and you see the whole system speaking through him.
'Flouted by a man like your father' — that's a very precise social observation.
Lawyer Wakem is the kind of figure who accumulates power through the legal system — and that system had very specific views about who was and was not suitable.
The Tullivers have been ruined partly through the courts — and now Tom, in confronting Philip, is using the logic of that same hierarchy to exclude Maggie.
He has internalised the values of the very system that destroyed his father.
That internalisation — James, that's the sharpest thing you could say about Tom Tulliver.
And Eliot gives us, in chapter fifty-five, her direct philosophical verdict on exactly this kind of moral formation.
She's writing about Tom without naming him — but every word lands on him like a verdict.

"The mysterious complexity of our life is not to be embraced by maxims, and that to lace ourselves up in formulas of that sort is to repress all the divine promptings and inspirations that spring from growing insight and sympathy."
Tom is the man of maxims made flesh.
He operates by ready-made rules — about family, about debt, about female behaviour — and never once troubles himself with the question of whether he has the insight to apply them.
And Eliot's fury at that — quiet, steady, devastating — is what drives the moral architecture of the whole novel.
'Lace ourselves up in formulas' — it's such a physical image, isn't it.
A corset of the mind. Eliot knew exactly what a corset felt like — and what it did to the body wearing it.
And there's something equally wonderful about Bob Jakin — who in a completely different register embodies the opposite of all this moral rigidity.
Bob operates entirely on instinct and charm — no formulas, no maxims, just the magnificent improvisation of a man who reads each situation fresh.
Listen to him working Mrs Glegg — it's practically a theatrical monologue.

"It's a thousand pities such a lady as you shouldn't deal with a packman, i' stead o' goin' into these newfangled shops, where there's half-a-dozen fine gents wi' their chins propped up wi' a stiff stock, a-looking like bottles wi' ornamental stoppers."
'Bottles with ornamental stoppers' — I defy anyone not to hear that and immediately picture six Victorian shop assistants.
Bob's speech is also, if you look at it closely, a perfectly accurate economic critique.
He's describing the overheads of the retail trade — rent, staff, markup — versus the direct commerce of the packman.
'Isn't forced to throttle himself till the lies are squeezed out on him' — there is something almost Marxian about that image, actually.
The shop assistant as a man deformed by the conditions of his employment — performing gentility while being economically crushed.
It's a superb passage because Bob is simultaneously flattering Mrs Glegg and telling the truth about capitalism.
He uses the language of authenticity — 'the natural way of getting goods' — to sell her something.
And yet the critique inside the salesmanship is real: those shop assistants are being exploited, squeezed into performances of respectability they can't afford.
Eliot doesn't ask you to take sides between Bob's charm and the shop assistants' plight — she holds both in view at once.
That capacity to hold contradictions in view — it seems to be Eliot's fundamental ethical method in this novel.
And it's precisely what Tom cannot do — what the world around Maggie cannot do.
In our next segment, we'll be turning to the novel's treatment of desire and respectability — and the terrible cost Maggie pays for having both an inner life and a body.
Stay with us.

segments.title: Irony and Comedy in the Tulliver Household: Finding Light in Darkness

utterances.text: Welcome back to The Mill on the Floss Unpacked.
Today we're turning to something that often gets overlooked in discussions of this novel — its comedy.
George Eliot is one of the great ironists in English fiction, and The Mill on the Floss is shot through with moments of piercing, sometimes devastating wit.
To explore that, I'm joined by three brilliant readers of this novel.
Oliver Trevelyan is an actor, writer, and the voice behind more classic audiobooks than anyone I know — he hears this prose the way it was meant to be heard.
Dr. Daniel Rosen is a cultural historian who reads every joke in a novel as a symptom of something much larger — and he's usually right.
And Prof. James Blackstone brings the legal and social historian's eye — he knows what these institutions actually were, which makes Eliot's satire land even harder.
Oliver, let's start with you — because I think you'd argue that Eliot is, among other things, a supremely gifted entertainer.
She absolutely is, and I think people forget that — or feel slightly guilty admitting it, as if enjoyment were somehow in poor taste when the subject matter is this grave.
But open almost any chapter and you find Eliot doing something technically extraordinary — she's building an ironical portrait so precise, so affectionate, and so lethal, all at once.
Take the introduction of the Rev. Walter Stelling.
Eliot gives us this broad-chested, flaxen-haired man of God, and within two sentences you already know everything about him.
She writes that he had
"an air of defiant self-confidence inclining to brazenness."
Inclining to brazenness — she doesn't say brazen outright, she says inclining to it, which is somehow far more damning.
The narrator is doing exactly what Stelling does — presenting itself with great confidence — and then quietly pulling the rug out.
What strikes me about that passage is how precisely Eliot identifies the machinery underneath the performance.
Stelling isn't just vain — he's calculating.
His theology is chosen because evangelicalism is, as Eliot puts it, "the telling thing" in that diocese.
The Church of England here is a career ladder, pure and simple.
And then she delivers the line that crystallises the entire logic of respectability in this novel.
"A clergyman who has such vigorous intentions naturally gets a little into debt at starting."
Naturally — that word is doing enormous work.
The debt isn't a moral failure; it's presented as a logical consequence of ambition.
Eliot is showing us how a whole class justifies its entitlement as inevitability.
And she's historically accurate about it, which makes the comedy sharper.
The grammar school mastership was a genuine prize in the early nineteenth century — a comfortable living that many ambitious clergymen competed for quite ruthlessly.
The detail of the wine, the grand piano, the superior flower-garden — Eliot isn't inventing the aspirational shopping list.
That is precisely the material culture a man in Stelling's position would feel entitled to display.
The joke lands because it's true.
And Stelling will, of course, make a catastrophic mess of Tom Tulliver's education — which is the real price of all that vigorous intention.
But what I love is that Eliot doesn't let the comedy swamp the tenderness.
There's a scene in the Stelling household — Tom playing with a sword and dropping it on his own foot — that begins as near-farce and ends as something genuinely affecting.
Maggie thinks he's dead.
"She couldn't sorrow yet that he had hurt his foot; it seemed as if all happiness lay in his being alive."
One sentence, and suddenly the whole register shifts.
That capacity — to move from comic satire to pure emotional truth in a breath — is what separates Eliot from the merely clever.
That shift is important because it shows where Eliot's sympathies actually rest.
The children are the real cost of Stelling's vanity — his incompetence shapes Tom's entire future.
And yet she never lets the satire become a simple verdict — she makes us feel the warmth between Tom and Maggie even as we see the institutional failure surrounding them.
Let's move to Bob Jakin, because I think Oliver has been waiting to talk about him.
Bob is one of the great comic performances in this novel — Oliver, what makes him so alive on the page?
Bob Jakin is a genius.
I don't say that lightly — he is one of the most completely realised comic characters in Victorian fiction, and he's a pedlar.
Eliot gives him this irresistible technique — he sells by pretending to discourage the purchase.
He pitches a piece of figured muslin to Mrs Glegg by telling her it's far too good for her to bother with.
"You might as well look at poor folks's victual, mum; it 'ud on'y take away your appetite."
The dialect, the rhythm, the sheer cheek of comparing fine muslin to poor people's food — it's a perfectly crafted comic aria.
And Mrs Glegg, of course, is putty in his hands — because he's appealing to precisely her vanity about economy.
Bob Jakin's sales technique is actually a well-documented strategy among itinerant traders of the period — the reverse pitch.
You flatter the customer by staging a reluctance to sell — implying the goods are too fine for a person of their modest means.
Eliot knew exactly what she was doing with Bob — he's a figure of genuine working-class intelligence navigating a system that has very little use for him.
The comedy doesn't diminish that — it's the form his intelligence takes.
And contrast Bob with someone like Stelling — both are self-promoters, both are performing a role.
But Stelling performs from a position of institutional protection — the Church, the marriage settlement, the grammar school.
Bob has nothing but his wit and his ability to read people — and he's more honest about what he's doing.
Eliot's comedy is often a class thermometer — the funnier a character is, the more clearly they reveal who actually has power and who is improvising survival.
That's very well put — and it makes me think of Philip Wakem, who operates in a completely different register.
There's a moment where Philip confronts his father, and it is not comic at all — it's almost savage.
He says to Wakem senior, with all the controlled contempt he can muster:
"You know best what satisfaction you would have, beyond that of gratifying a ridiculous rancor worthy only of wandering savages."
There's no comedy there — but there is the same sharp Eliot intelligence, now turned toward something that bleeds.
Philip's line is interesting legally as well as emotionally.
The elder Wakem's rancor is rooted in the lawsuit — in a formal legal grievance — but Philip strips it of all legal dignity with that phrase "wandering savages."
He's saying: this isn't justice, this is tribalism.
And the fact that Philip — physically marginalised, socially constrained — is the one who has to say it gives it a particular force.
Before we move on, I want to come back to something Oliver raised — this idea that Eliot can be funny and devastating in the same breath.
There's a passage involving Stephen Guest that I think demonstrates that perfectly — Oliver, do you want to take that one?
Oh, the dog-stroking scene.
This is Eliot in absolute command of tone — she's playing Stephen Guest's paralysed desire for comedy while also making us feel how suffocating that desire is for Maggie.
Stephen, unable to speak or act, is reduced to pulling a dog's ears, and the narrator remarks that it was
"not a suggestive remark, and as the speaker did not follow it up by further development, it naturally left the conversation at a standstill."
The dry understatement is perfectly calibrated — she's describing the collapse of all communication while sounding like a polite review of a failed dinner party.
But then she gives us what Stephen actually wants — and here the comedy evaporates entirely.

"he only wished he dared look at Maggie, and that she would look at him,—let him have one long look into those deep, strange eyes of hers, and then he would be satisfied and quite reasonable after that"
Quite reasonable after that — and we know, of course, that he would not be.
That passage shows exactly what makes the Stephen Guest plot so uncomfortable to read — Eliot is genuinely funny about his obsession, but she never lets you forget what it costs Maggie.
Maggie has no distinct thought — just the sense of a presence like a hovering bird in darkness.
Stephen gets three paragraphs of interiority; Maggie gets a metaphor of enclosure.
The comedy is how we get into the room; the asymmetry is what we find when we're there.
That's a remarkable way to end that thought — comedy as the door, and darkness waiting behind it.
In our next segment we'll be looking at the Dodson family in full cry — which I suspect will give all three of you rather a lot to work with.

segments.title: Catastrophe and Class: The Economics of Ruin in Industrial England

utterances.text: Welcome to The Mill on the Floss Unpacked.
I'm your host, and today we're diving into one of the novel's great preoccupations: the economics of ruin, and what catastrophe reveals about class, pride, and the people it destroys.
With me today are three remarkable minds who each bring something distinct and indispensable to this conversation.
Dr. Daniel Rosen is a cultural historian who reads novels as anatomies of class power — and he is going to show us exactly what the Tulliver ruin looks like when you follow the money.
Prof. James Blackstone is a legal and social historian — the man who can tell you precisely what it meant, in Victorian England, to lose a lawsuit and everything that followed from it.
And Oliver Trevelyan — actor, writer, and the voice of more classic audiobooks than I dare count — brings us the prose itself, read with the relish it deserves.
Let's begin with the spark that lights the fuse: Mr Tulliver's extraordinary letter to Mrs Glegg.
This letter is one of the great comic grenades in the novel.
Mrs Glegg has worked herself into a magnificent posture of magnanimity — she is prepared, at great personal cost, to forgive.
And then Tulliver writes to tell her she needn't trouble her mind about her five hundred pounds — it'll be returned within the month, with interest.
The timing is exquisite — Eliot waits until Mrs Glegg is at her most self-congratulatory before dropping the letter into her lap.
And then comes the line that finishes her off — Tulliver says she was welcome to his house whenever she liked to come,
"but he desired no favours from her, either for himself or his children."
The courtesy in the first half makes the dismissal in the second half all the more devastating.
He's not being rude — he's being perfectly civil — and that is the most insulting thing he could possibly do to a Dodson.
It's also economically significant, and that's easy to miss if you're laughing too hard.
The five hundred pounds Mrs Glegg holds is not simply a family loan — it represents a particular kind of leverage that middle-class women of her station could exercise over male relatives.
Her money, kept in her own control, is her independence and her power within the family structure.
By repaying it — or claiming he will repay it — Tulliver is not just rejecting her charity; he is severing the financial tie that gives her standing in his household.
The comedy Eliot orchestrates here is perfectly precise — she knows exactly what each party is fighting over, and it isn't goodwill.
And this is where Eliot's satire gets genuinely uncomfortable — because Tulliver's proud refusal is also the decision that ruins him.
He borrows money to fight a lawsuit — money he doesn't have, from a lawyer he despises — in order to assert a masculine dignity the system has already determined to deny him.
Eliot is careful to show us that his hatred of Wakem is not irrational — it is the only legible form his powerlessness is allowed to take.
Listen to how she renders his contempt for this man who always seems to be winning —
"A hook-nosed glib fellow! as cool as a cucumber, — always looking so sure of his game!"
That is not the voice of a calculating man — it is the voice of someone the system has made helpless, and who has nowhere to put his rage except onto the face of one lawyer.
The law isn't neutral in this novel — it is Wakem, and Wakem is what the law looks like to the people it defeats.
"Cool as a cucumber" — you feel the years of accumulated indignation packed into that phrase.

Eliot has a remarkable ear for the particular idiom in which a man nurses a grievance — he doesn't hate Wakem in the abstract; he hates the hook nose and the glibness, the physical presence of the man.
And then there's Mrs Tulliver's contribution to the catastrophe — which Eliot renders with this wonderfully mischievous passage about feathers.
She sets up the proverbial feather that breaks the camel's back — and then immediately insists we not blame the feather,
"it might even be comparable to that proverbial feather which has the credit or discredit of breaking the camel's back."
The "credit or discredit" — that little pivot — is pure Eliot; she refuses to let the comic image settle into a simple moral.
Mrs Tulliver is simultaneously being gently mocked and gently defended within the same grammatical construction.
That passage does something quietly important about the position of wives under nineteenth-century law and custom.
Eliot's narrator is careful to say that Mrs Tulliver's influence does not operate through her "single personality" — it operates through her function as a Dodson.
She is legible to her husband not as an individual with views, but as the representative of a clan whose authority he has vowed to resist.
Which means the more she urges caution, the more he is compelled toward recklessness — simply to prove he is not dominated.
It's a mechanism Eliot understands from the inside, and it is not comic when you follow it to its conclusion.
And the conclusion arrives in the auction — in what is sold, and who loses it.
The passage where Mrs Tulliver goes through her linens is one of the most devastating pieces of social critique Eliot ever wrote — and it is almost entirely in dialect.
She is cataloguing her own dispossession — the labour of her hands, her identity, her claim to pass something on to her children — being dissolved into commodity.
Listen to what she says about where these cloths came from —
"To think o' these cloths as I spun myself... and Job Haxey wove 'em, and brought the piece home on his back."
That chain of labour — spun, woven, carried home on a man's back — is not sentiment; it is the record of work that produced value, and that value is now being expropriated.
And it will go into strange people's houses, and "perhaps be cut with the knives, and wore out before I'm dead."
The marker stitch that cannot be removed without cutting the cloth — that is the detail of a novelist who knows exactly what she is doing.
"They must cut the cloth to get it out" — I find that extraordinary every time I read it.
Her identity is literally woven in — and the only way to erase it is an act of destruction.
It's also worth noting that Mrs Tulliver — usually so passive, as the narrator says — is suddenly animated by this loss in a way she never is by her husband's legal battles.
The linen is hers — really hers, made by her hands — and its sale reaches a part of her that nothing else has touched.
Eliot does something cruel and generous simultaneously there — she gives this woman her one moment of authentic feeling, and it is entirely about things.
The auction of household goods following insolvency was, in this period, a genuinely brutal instrument.
Everything — and I mean everything — could be taken: furniture, tools, stock, the contents of linen cupboards, sometimes the clothes on your back.
The creditors' legal right was absolute, and the family had no protection beyond whatever informal mercy the assignees chose to extend.
Mrs Tulliver's linen was not a luxury item — it was a form of stored wealth, of security, the closest thing a woman of her class had to independent capital.
When it goes, her future goes with it — and Eliot makes sure we understand the precise material weight of that loss.
And then Eliot takes this economics of ruin and internalises it — turns it on Maggie herself.
Because what Maggie faces in that extraordinary chapter of temptation is not just a moral choice — it is a choice between two forms of impoverishment.
Either she renounces love, wealth, ease — everything her nature craves — or she keeps them at the cost of destroying the faculty in herself that makes her Maggie.
Eliot finds a metaphor for this that is quite shocking in its precision —
"She might as well hope to enjoy walking by maiming her feet, as hope to enjoy an existence in which she set out by maiming the faith and sympathy that were the best organs of her soul."
"Maiming" — twice — it is a word of violence, of permanent damage, not of mild moral compromise.
Eliot is saying: what would be lost if Maggie chose Stephen is not merely Lucy's happiness — it is Maggie's capacity for the very thing that makes her worth reading about.
The ruin of the Tulliver family was economic — this ruin would be ontological.
The word "organs" catches me every time — faith and sympathy as organs of the soul.
It's biological, almost medical — which is exactly right, because Eliot wants us to understand this as a physiological fact about Maggie, not a pious sentiment.
And underneath all that turbulence — the fierce battle of emotions, the temptation, the guilt — there is a kind of terrible quiet in how Eliot describes her externally.
She moves with "quiescence and even torpor" — while inside, as Eliot says, "all the worst evil in her had lain in ambush till now."
That gap between surface calm and interior catastrophe — that is the real inheritance of the Tulliver ruin.
I want to stay with that inheritance — because it arrives in the most brutal form in Tom's rejection of Maggie.
What Tom says to her is worth hearing in full, because every sentence in it is doing a different kind of damage.
"You have disgraced us all. You have disgraced my father's name. You have been a curse to your best friends. You have been base, deceitful; no motives are strong enough to restrain you."
"I wash my hands of you forever. You don't belong to me."
The "name" — his father's name — is doing the most work there.
Tom has spent years reconstructing the family's financial reputation after the ruin, and in his accounting Maggie has just destroyed it again.
He doesn't distinguish between financial disgrace and moral disgrace — for a Tulliver of his formation, they are the same thing.
"You don't belong to me" — that is the sentence that haunts me most in this passage.
Because belonging — family, property, name, the Tulliver mill itself — is precisely what the novel has shown to be contingent, precarious, always under threat.
Tom says "you don't belong to me" as if belonging were something he could simply revoke — but the novel has already shown us that no one in this family truly belongs to anything.
The mill is gone. The name is compromised. The linen is in strangers' houses.
What Tom is protecting, with his trembling rage, is a fiction of respectability that the system has already sold off at auction.
"Tremulous rage" — Eliot doesn't let Tom be simply monstrous.
The trembling is important — it tells us he is not cold, not calculated; he is frightened and furious and broken, and this is the only language he has for it.
That's actually what makes it unbearable — not the cruelty of a villain, but the rigid grief of someone who learned to feel only through the categories the world gave him.
And Maggie knows it — which is why, when it comes, the flood is not only a catastrophe.
That feels like exactly the right note on which to move forward — the catastrophe that is also, in its terrible way, a resolution.
We've traced the ruin from its comic origins in Tulliver's letter, through the auction of the linen, to its final form in Tom's verdict on his sister.
In the next segment, we'll be asking what the novel imagines as the alternatives — and whether Eliot believes any escape was ever truly possible.

segments.title: The Narrative Voice: How Eliot Guides Us Through Moral Complexity

utterances.text: Welcome back to The Mill on the Floss Unpacked.
This segment turns to something that sits at the very heart of what makes this novel extraordinary: the narrator's voice.
George Eliot is not content to simply show us her characters — she guides us, nudges us, and occasionally ambushes us with a perfectly placed irony.
And nowhere is that narrative intelligence more alive than in the passages about Maggie and Tom's childhood.
Oliver Trevelyan — who has spent more time inside this prose than perhaps anyone — is going to lead us into the text.
James Blackstone will ground us in what the social world of this novel actually felt like to live in.
And Daniel Rosen will remind us, with characteristic force, who the system is actually built to serve.
Oliver — the gypsy episode. Let's begin there.
The gypsy episode is Eliot at her most deliciously comic — and her most quietly devastating.
You have this small furious child, humiliated by Tom, sitting on the roots of a tree and deciding that her entire life must now change.
And the narrator sets it up with such perfect deadpan control.
She writes: "Maggie's intentions, as usual, were on a larger scale than Tom imagined."
"No! she would run away and go to the gypsies, and Tom should never see her any more."
That exclamation mark — "No!" — that is Maggie's voice breaking through the narrator's.
Eliot gives us the child's interior drama in the child's own register, and then immediately steps back with this amused, tender irony.
That double consciousness — child and observer, comedy and sympathy — is the whole technique of the novel in miniature.
What strikes me about that passage — and Oliver is exactly right about the technique — is the social precision underneath the comedy.
Maggie has been told repeatedly that she is "like a gypsy" and "half wild."
Those are not neutral descriptions — in the mid-nineteenth century they are a form of social classification, a warning.
And what does Maggie do with this language that has been used to diminish her?
She reclaims it — she takes the label and constructs from it an entire alternative world where she would be respected.
The narrator tells us the gypsies would "gladly receive her and pay her much respect on account of her superior knowledge."
There is something both comic and genuinely poignant in that fantasy of recognition — it is what Maggie will spend the entire novel searching for.
And the narrator is completely aware of that irony — she earns it through the most precise social observation.
There's a passage that follows the gypsy escape which I think is one of the most remarkable things in the novel.
The narrator turns to address us directly about Maggie's education — or rather, the education she was never given.
"in travelling over her small mind you would have found the most unexpected ignorance as well as unexpected knowledge."
"Her thoughts generally were the oddest mixture of clear-eyed acumen and blind dreams."
That phrase — "clear-eyed acumen and blind dreams" — is Eliot's structural diagnosis of what Victorian education did to girls.
You develop a child's genuine intelligence and then systematically deprive her of the knowledge that would make it useful.
The comedy is real — Maggie deducing the meaning of 'poly' from dictionary study is genuinely funny.
But the joke is not on Maggie — it is on the world that left her with a dictionary and called that an education.
That's exactly it — the comic mode is the vehicle for the moral charge.
And the same technique operates brilliantly in what happens next — when Maggie's fantasy curdles into terror.
She arrives among the gypsies and within minutes — within minutes — the rescue fantasy has become a horror story.
The narrator delivers the turn with glorious precision:
"she had begun to think that they meant perhaps to kill her as soon as it was dark, and cut up her body for gradual cooking."
"Gradual cooking" — those two words.
The specificity is everything — it is a child's imagination at full, baroque stretch.
And then, immediately, the narrator gives us the philosophical punchline: the thing Maggie most dreads is offending the gypsies by revealing her opinion of them.
She suspects they are cannibals but she does not wish to be rude. That is Maggie Tulliver in a sentence.
And the narrator goes further still — she notes that Maggie wonders whether the Devil, if present, would know her thoughts.
The narrator tells us this is considered "with a keenness of interest that no theologian could have exceeded."
That comparison to a theologian is not merely comic — it is Eliot insisting on the seriousness of Maggie's intelligence even at its most feverish.
The narrator never condescends to Maggie — she laughs with her, not at her.
And that distinction — laughing with rather than at — is precisely what gives Eliot's irony its moral force throughout the novel.
That same care for the interior life of the humiliated appears in the Tom passages — and it's equally rigorous.
Tom at Stelling's school is being crushed by an educational system designed for a completely different kind of mind.
And the narrator — characteristically — does something unexpected: she tells us this suffering made Tom "more like a girl than he had ever been in his life before."
That is not a casual phrase.
Eliot is using Tom's humiliation to make us feel what Maggie lives with every single day — the vulnerability of being told you are wrong simply by existing.
The narrator is working on us — building empathy for Tom precisely by connecting his suffering to Maggie's permanent condition.
And then comes one of the most quietly devastating moments in the whole novel — Tom's prayer.
This boy who has broken down over Latin conjugations — five times, on the supines of the third conjugation, no less — reaches the end of his resources.
He has tried everything he can think of — and there is something both tender and comic in the narrator telling us he considered rapping his head against the wall.
But Tom is not given to hypothesis and experiment — so he turns, shyly, to prayer.
And Eliot gives us the exact words, in that low whisper:
"and please to make me always remember my Latin."
"And make Mr Stelling say I sha'n't do Euclid any more. Amen."
The "Amen" finishes it.
It's heartbreaking and it's funny and you cannot separate those two things — and that is exactly what this narrator does with every child in this book.
What you're all tracing is a narrator who holds irony and tenderness in the same breath — never letting either collapse into the other.
That moral intelligence — guiding us without hectoring us — is, I think, what makes this novel feel so alive more than a century and a half after it was written.
We're going to carry that question — how the narrator shapes our sympathies — into the next part of our conversation.

segments.title: Closing: Drowning in Duty—Love, Sacrifice, and Redemption

utterances.text: We've arrived at the end of our journey through The Mill on the Floss.
And it feels right to close where the novel itself closes — with loss, with water, and with questions that don't quite resolve.
George Eliot opens her story in a kind of dream — and ends it in catastrophe.
James, Oliver, Daniel — I want to ask each of you: what does this novel finally say about duty, sacrifice, and what it costs a person to be good?
I think we have to start where the novel starts — which is, genuinely, in a reverie.
The narrator shakes herself awake at the very opening, and what she says is quietly extraordinary.

"Ah, my arms are really benumbed. I have been pressing my elbows on the arms of my chair, and dreaming that I was standing on the bridge in front of Dorlcote Mill, as it looked one February afternoon many years ago."
The entire novel is framed as a dream that has numbed the dreamer.
Memory, for Eliot, is not a comfort — it is a physical affliction.
And that primes us, I think, for everything that follows: a story told from the vantage point of irreparable loss.
It's a brilliant piece of theatre, that opening — the narrator catching herself mid-daydream.
You feel the jolt of it: one moment we're on the bridge at Dorlcote Mill, the next we're back in a parlour chair.
But what I keep returning to is how early on we see the seeds of the tragedy — and how small and domestic those seeds are.
Take the scene with young Maggie and Lucy — Eliot sets it up with such lightness, and then slips the knife in.
"Maggie would have thought a little while ago that she could never be cross with pretty little Lucy, any more than she could be cruel to a little white mouse."
The white mouse! Eliot is so good at that — the image that is simultaneously comic and devastating.
Because here is the entire arc of the novel, compressed into a child's jealousy over a cousin.
Oliver is right that the arc is there early — but I want to be precise about what kind of arc it is.
Maggie's jealousy over Tom's attention to Lucy isn't simply a character flaw — it's a symptom of deprivation.
She's a girl who has been systematically denied — by her family, by her education, by the whole social structure — the recognition she craves.
So when Tom turns toward Lucy, even briefly, it registers as catastrophic abandonment.
And then the novel asks Maggie to renounce even the one thing she finally reaches for — love, connection, Stephen Guest.
The cost of that renunciation is spelled out in language that I find almost unbearable in its precision.
"Faithfulness and constancy mean something else besides doing what is easiest and pleasantest to ourselves. They mean renouncing whatever is opposed to the reliance others have in us."
Eliot gives Maggie the most rigorous moral intelligence in the novel — and then uses that intelligence to destroy her.
That word — reliance — is doing enormous work in that passage, and I don't think we should rush past it.
In the legal and social world Eliot is describing, a woman's entire existence is structured around the reliance others place in her.
She has no independent legal standing, no financial autonomy, no public life.
What she has is her reputation and the emotional trust of those around her — and that, for Maggie, is everything.
And Eliot is unflinching about the self-accusation Maggie directs at herself: weak, selfish, hard.
The question the novel refuses to answer cleanly is whether that verdict is just — or whether the system has made Maggie indict herself for the system's crime.
That cry for Lucy — "Think of her" — those two words at the end of the speech are where I always feel the floor give way.
Eliot has been building this great rhetorical edifice, these long syntactical periods about duty and constancy — and then she breaks it with two syllables.
"Think of her——" — that double dash is a stage direction, as far as I'm concerned.
It says: she cannot go on. The sentence has broken, and so has she.
And then the flood comes — in every sense — and the novel answers grief with annihilation.
The ending has always divided readers, and I think it should.
There's a reading in which the flood is merciful — it reunites Maggie and Tom in the moment before death, and that reunion is the emotional resolution the novel has been building toward.
And then there's the reading I can't shake: that drowning is the only exit the novel's world permits for a woman like Maggie.
The coda Eliot writes for the aftermath is devastating precisely because it refuses consolation.
"Nature repairs her ravages, but not all. To the eyes that have dwelt on the past, there is no thorough repair."
Not all. No thorough repair. Eliot will not let us off the hook with a symmetrical ending.
The scarred hills remain scarred. That is the novel's final moral statement.
"The uptorn trees are not rooted again" — I think that line is as good a description of grief as any in the English language.
And it lands differently once you understand the novel is itself framed as an act of memory — that dreaming narrator pressing her elbows on the chair.
Someone has been carrying this story for years. The weight of it has gone physical — numbed arms, a body that has held its grief in a particular shape.
That is what irreparable loss does, Eliot says. It doesn't disappear. It settles into the posture of the person who carries it.
I want to say something in defence of the ending that might sound perverse.
The flood is formally outrageous — it arrives like a plot device, and critics have never entirely forgiven Eliot for it.
But emotionally — as a performer, as someone who has lived inside this prose — it feels inevitable.
Maggie has been drowning for the whole book. The river is simply honest enough to finish what the world began.
Drowning for the whole book. That phrase will stay with me.
James, Daniel, Oliver — you've given this novel the reading it deserves: rigorous, tender, and unflinching in equal measure.
The Mill on the Floss is a novel about the cost of conscience — what it means to love people who have been shaped by the same forces that are slowly destroying you.
And it asks, without ever quite answering: what does faithfulness owe to the self?
Thank you for listening to The Mill on the Floss Unpacked.
The water rises. The hills bear their scars. And the novel endures.

Mr Glegg on his side, too, had a double source of mental occupation, which
gave every promise of being inexhaustible. On the one hand, he surprised
himself by his discoveries in natural history, finding that his piece of
garden-ground contained wonderful caterpillars, slugs, and insects, which, so
far as he had heard, had never before attracted human observation; and he
noticed remarkable coincidences between these zoological phenomena and the
great events of that time,—as, for example, that before the burning of
York Minster there had been mysterious serpentine marks on the leaves of the
rose-trees, together with an unusual prevalence of slugs, which he had been
puzzled to know the meaning of, until it flashed upon him with this melancholy
conflagration. (Mr Glegg had an unusual amount of mental activity, which, when
disengaged from the wool business, naturally made itself a pathway in other
directions.) And his second subject of meditation was the
“contrairiness” of the female mind, as typically exhibited in Mrs
Glegg. That a creature made—in a genealogical sense—out of a
man’s rib, and in this particular case maintained in the highest
respectability without any trouble of her own, should be normally in a state of
contradiction to the blandest propositions and even to the most accommodating
concessions, was a mystery in the scheme of things to which he had often in
vain sought a clew in the early chapters of Genesis. Mr Glegg had chosen the
eldest Miss Dodson as a handsome embodiment of female prudence and thrift, and
being himself of a money-getting, money-keeping turn, had calculated on much
conjugal harmony. But in that curious compound, the feminine character, it may
easily happen that the flavour is unpleasant in spite of excellent ingredients;
and a fine systematic stinginess may be accompanied with a seasoning that quite
spoils its relish. Now, good Mr Glegg himself was stingy in the most amiable
manner; his neighbours called him “near,” which always means that
the person in question is a lovable skinflint. If you expressed a preference
for cheese-parings, Mr Glegg would remember to save them for you, with a
good-natured delight in gratifying your palate, and he was given to pet all
animals which required no appreciable keep. There was no humbug or hypocrisy
about Mr Glegg; his eyes would have watered with true feeling over the sale of
a widow’s furniture, which a five-pound note from his side pocket would
have prevented; but a donation of five pounds to a person “in a small way
of life” would have seemed to him a mad kind of lavishness rather than
“charity,” which had always presented itself to him as a
contribution of small aids, not a neutralizing of misfortune. And Mr Glegg was
just as fond of saving other people’s money as his own; he would have
ridden as far round to avoid a turnpike when his expenses were to be paid for
him, as when they were to come out of his own pocket, and was quite zealous in
trying to induce indifferent acquaintances to adopt a cheap substitute for
blacking. This inalienable habit of saving, as an end in itself, belonged to
the industrious men of business of a former generation, who made their fortunes
slowly, almost as the tracking of the fox belongs to the harrier,—it
constituted them a “race,” which is nearly lost in these days of
rapid money-getting, when lavishness comes close on the back of want. In
old-fashioned times an “independence” was hardly ever made without
a little miserliness as a condition, and you would have found that quality in
every provincial district, combined with characters as various as the fruits
from which we can extract acid. The true Harpagons were always marked and
exceptional characters; not so the worthy tax-payers, who, having once pinched
from real necessity, retained even in the midst of their comfortable
retirement, with their wallfruit and wine-bins, the habit of regarding life as
an ingenious process of nibbling out one’s livelihood without leaving any
perceptible deficit, and who would have been as immediately prompted to give up
a newly taxed luxury when they had had their clear five hundred a year, as when
they had only five hundred pounds of capital. Mr Glegg was one of these men,
found so impracticable by chancellors of the exchequer; and knowing this, you
will be the better able to understand why he had not swerved from the
conviction that he had made an eligible marriage, in spite of the too pungent
seasoning that nature had given to the eldest Miss Dodson’s virtues. A
man with an affectionate disposition, who finds a wife to concur with his
fundamental idea of life, easily comes to persuade himself that no other woman
would have suited him so well, and does a little daily snapping and quarrelling
without any sense of alienation. Mr Glegg, being of a reflective turn, and no
longer occupied with wool, had much wondering meditation on the peculiar
constitution of the female mind as unfolded to him in his domestic life; and
yet he thought Mrs Glegg’s household ways a model for her sex. It struck
him as a pitiable irregularity in other women if they did not roll up their
table-napkins with the same tightness and emphasis as Mrs Glegg did, if their
pastry had a less leathery consistence, and their damson cheese a less
venerable hardness than hers; nay, even the peculiar combination of grocery and
druglike odors in Mrs Glegg’s private cupboard impressed him as the only
right thing in the way of cupboard smells. I am not sure that he would not have
longed for the quarrelling again, if it had ceased for an entire week; and it
is certain that an acquiescent, mild wife would have left his meditations
comparatively jejune and barren of mystery.
c12:p6.summary: Mr Glegg finds mystery in caterpillars and slugs while remaining bewildered by his wife's contradictions; he practices amiable thrift and loves order, having married for conjugal harmony but finding seasoning that spoils the relish.
